new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: group-level-statement. Ehret's claim is about the Rift subgroup ('tone.. has ceased to be phonologically significant in the Rift languages', loss dated to proto-Rift); the only Asa-specific sentence (p.131) concerns re-phonemicizing Winter's transcription and says nothing about tone or stress. Google Books snippets only. | checker: Google Books volume uhMOAAAAYAAJ resolves (403/'automated queries' block by automated download today, so no new search-within-volume queries were possible; not reachable by automated download, Books API 429). A's saved extract read in full: every fragment of A's quote is present at the stated pages (p.40 'tone, with a few exceptions, has ceased t…
new_statements.relation_note: Ch. 4 reconstructs PSC tone from Dahalo and Ma'a because Rift lost distinctive tone; hypothesises PSC was 'only just beginning to shift from stress to tone' (p.42).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level claim: distinctive lexical tone was lost in proto-Rift, so Rift languages (which include Asa) have no phonologically significant tone; word 'tone' is predictable/syntactically determined intonation (described for Iraqw and Kw'adza: nouns in isolation high..falling-penult..low-final / Kw'adza high-low-low). Nothing is said about Asa's own accent or intonation, and Winter's Asa transcription was reduced to 'tentative phonemicizations' without a remark on tone/stress marking (no hit for 'Asa stress' or 'accent').
new_statements.exceptions: 'with a few exceptions' (p.40, unspecified in snippets; p.40 also mentions loan nouns from Dadog heard 'not as tone but as stress' in a West Rift context)
new_statements.identity_note: Asa in Ehret 1980 = Winter's 1974 Aasáx data + Merker's vocabulary, i.e. this languoid; but the prosodic statement found is made for 'the Rift languages' as a group (Rift = Kw'adza, Asa, Iraqw, Burunge, Alagwa, p. 20), with East Rift explicitly 'less well known' and only Kw'adza's patterns actually described. Not tagged to aasa1238 in Glottolog's reference list (it is in Glottolog under other South Cushitic languages).
